dos: AGENTS.md must identify the repository and its purpose.
AGENTS.md must state the repository scope and important boundaries.
Project-specific rules may add requirements without weakening shared rules unless authorized.
AGENTS.md must state required files and structure when those requirements apply to the repository type.
AGENTS.md must identify which instructions apply repository-wide and which apply to subdirectories.
AGENTS.md must tell contributors to read README.md, AGENTS.md, and applicable documentation before changing files.
AGENTS.md must list the repository's applicable validation commands.
AGENTS.md must state applicable security and secret-handling rules.
AGENTS.md must document intentional deviations from shared conventions.
AGENTS.md instructions must be actionable, current, and concise.
AGENTS.md must keep credentials, secrets, and private machine-specific paths out of its contents.
Every documentation-only repository must extend the general AGENTS.md requirements with applicable documentation guidance.
After the seven general AGENTS.md headings, add a ## Documentation section. Document documentation scope, authority boundaries, indexes, link validation, and documentation-only limits.

Documentation-only README.md must add Scope, Authority, Navigation, Contribution, and Documentation validation, in that order, for repository scope, authoritative sources, indexes, contribution/setup requirements, and link/document validation. Place these headings in the profile extension area defined by general.json and include them in the Table of Contents.
Documentation-only README.md must link every authoritative documentation surface from its indexes.
Deterministic validation must verify that every documented surface, index link, structured-document path, and embedded reference resolves to its intended target.
The Docs authority map must validate repository entries, directive namespaces, structured-document paths, and reciprocal authority references when the referenced checkout is available.
Every workspace repository must extend the general AGENTS.md requirements with applicable workspace guidance.
After the seven general AGENTS.md headings, add a ## Workspace section. Document workspace purpose, role boundaries, communication, runbooks, recovery, and validation.
Store each workspace-owned runbook as a separate JSON file under runbooks/.
Require runbooks/README.md as the navigation-only overview and index for every runbook file.
Require each runbook record to contain id, purpose, owner, boundaries, and steps.
Use runbooks/<name>.json#id=<stable-id> for machine-verifiable references.
Keep each procedure authoritative in one location and link to it from indexes.
Keep company-wide task status, assignment, sequencing, blockers, milestones, and next actions in Tasklist.
Keep workspace-specific decisions and durable policy in directives.json or the applicable structured directive file.
Keep local operational procedures in runbooks/ and reference Operations for company-wide workflows.

Workspace README.md must add Authority, Runbooks, Communication, and Recovery, in that order, identifying ownership, operational boundaries, runbook navigation, communication channels, and recovery ownership. Place these headings in the profile extension area defined by general.json and include them in the Table of Contents.
Deterministic validation must validate every runbooks/*.json record against the workspace runbook contract and require non-empty id, purpose, owner, boundaries, and steps fields.
Deterministic validation must validate every machine-followable runbooks/<name>.json#id=<stable-id> reference against the referenced record.
Workspace README indexes must link runbooks/README.md and every authoritative structured directive collection.
Every application repository must extend the general AGENTS.md requirements with applicable application guidance.
Applications must validate configuration before opening connections, make shutdown repeatable, and test every externally observable workflow.
Applications must provide a root README.md, document runtime configuration and user-visible workflows, and provide .env.example when environment configuration is supported.

Application README.md must add Configuration and Operations, in that order, documenting startup and shutdown, runtime settings and defaults (or explicitly stating that no runtime configuration exists), externally observable workflows, and operational boundaries. Place these headings in the profile extension area defined by general.json and include them in the Table of Contents.

After the seven general AGENTS.md headings, add a ## Application section. Document the actual runtime entrypoint(s), lifecycle behavior, runtime configuration sources/defaults (or that none exist), and safe operational boundaries; distinguish these from package metadata and deployment configuration.
docs/ must contain the complete end-user documentation for the application; docs/README.md must provide its overview and index and index every end-user document.
Application repositories must link docs/README.md from the root README.md.
Application package.json must declare its runtime/start entrypoints, environment contract, and private/public distribution status when applicable.

Application repositories may include examples/ when it improves user documentation; when present, examples/README.md must index runnable examples and each example must document prerequisites, commands, and expected results.

Public npm repositories must contain exactly one publication workflow at .github/workflows/publish.yml in addition to .github/workflows/ci.yml; no other GitHub Actions workflow files are allowed. If GHCR publication is also applied, both publication profiles use this single publish.yml file.

Publication workflows must use the GitHub Actions tag filter `v[0-9]+.[0-9]+.[0-9]+` so only three-component numeric version-shaped tags start the workflow, verify that the tag exactly matches package.json, and require successful Ubuntu validation before npm publication.

An npm publication workflow must be separate from the general validation workflow, inherit general.json validation requirements, and publish only after the required Ubuntu validation and exact tag/package-version checks succeed.

An npm publication job must grant only the contents: read and id-token: write permissions needed for checkout and npm provenance, and the Operations release handoff must verify that the exact package version is available from the public registry before reporting publication complete.
Private-repository CI must contain validation only; any authorized GHCR publication must be isolated to exact v#.#.# tags and separately approved.
After publication, use a separate Operations release handoff and a separate GitOps deployment handoff for any rollout; publication alone must not deploy the image.

AGENTS.md must document the Node.js version, runtime commands, runtime environment configuration (or state that none exists), module system, and Node-specific validation. Distinguish runtime environment settings from package metadata and CLI arguments.

An Eli-approved emergency exemption must be recorded in package.json.eliware.exempt with this rule ID, reason, approver, approval timestamp, and either a concrete expiry date for a temporary exemption or expiry:null for a permanent exemption.
When a repository declares typechecking or a production build capability, define explicit read-only typecheck and build validation commands and keep generated output outside the repository.
CI must execute applicable typecheck and production-build validation before publication.
Use the shared canonical Prettier configuration for maintained Node.js repositories.
Deterministic validation must enforce unique directive IDs, valid parent-child ID prefixes, E-only ancestry for E-rules, and an E ancestor for every A-rule.
A repository's root directive namespace must match the namespace assigned to it by the authoritative repository registry when that registry entry exists.
Every repository must use .gitignore rules that exclude dependencies, VCS state, coverage, build output, runtime state, secrets, and machine-specific files.
CI validation consists of npm ci followed by npm test; npm test is the repository's aggregate deterministic gate.
eliware-test owns lint and format validation invoked by npm test; CI workflows must not duplicate those checks.
Keep CodeScope out of GitHub CI, Knit validation, TagIt preflight, and other automatic validation workflows.

specs/ must contain specs/README.md as its overview and index, authority.json as the local authority registry, one or more directives.json files, and any applicable indexed structured specification records.
specs/README.md must link every authority.json, directives.json, and applicable structured specification file and identify the authority represented by each.
The normative contents of specs/ must be indexed JSON specification records; README.md, authority.json, directives.json, and applicable structured specifications are permitted.
Each release entry must summarize user-visible changes and include breaking changes, migration, or security information when applicable; update it before release validation.
README.md must link RELEASE_NOTES.md from Links when the file exists.
Treat the applicable convention profiles and their directive IDs as the sole authority for repository requirements.
Every library repository must extend the general AGENTS.md requirements with applicable library guidance.

After the seven general AGENTS.md headings, add a ## Library section. Document public API boundaries, exports and declarations, compatibility policy, package contents/allowlist, package validation, typecheck, and consumer-validation commands.

Libraries must define explicit exports and declarations for typed public APIs, test the public API, use package allowlists, and provide .env.example when the library supports environment configuration.
Every library must contain examples/README.md and at least one runnable example under examples/.
Every library must contain docs/ with complete end-user documentation and docs/README.md as its overview and index.

Public Eliware packages must use the @eliware scope, repository metadata matching package.json, an approved license, the Eliware Discord, GitHub, and eliware@eliware.org support channels, and synchronized public branding.

Library README.md must add API, Packaging, and Examples, in that order, including installation, public exports, compatibility, package validation, and at least one runnable usage example. Place these headings in the profile extension area defined by general.json and include them in the Table of Contents.
Library README.md must link docs/README.md and examples/README.md when those surfaces are required, and every runnable example must state prerequisites, command, and expected result.
Library package.json must declare the public entrypoint or exports, typed declaration metadata when applicable, and an intentional package file allowlist.
Libraries may contain examples only when useful outside the mandatory library example contract; non-library repositories may also use examples when useful and must index them when present.
Every web application repository must extend the application AGENTS.md requirements with applicable web guidance.

After the seven general AGENTS.md headings, add a ## Web section. Document routes and route ownership, assets and public root, runtime/build configuration, development-server ports, browser validation commands, build output paths, and deployment boundaries. State explicitly when any of these categories does not apply.

Web README.md must add Configuration, Routes, Assets, Development server, Build, and Deployment, in that order, documenting runtime settings, ports, public asset root, browser validation, build output, and deployment boundaries. Configuration merges with the application Configuration heading required by application.json. Place these headings in the profile extension area defined by general.json and include them in the Table of Contents.
Deterministic validation must inspect version-controlled paths for secret-like files and reject unauthorized matches.
A tracked-file exception must identify the exact path, rule ID, approver, reason, and expiry or review condition in package.json.eliware.exempt.
Every CLI repository must extend the general AGENTS.md requirements with applicable CLI guidance.

After the seven general AGENTS.md headings, add a ## CLI section. Document each executable entrypoint and its target; command/subcommand names; option and positional-argument parsing, defaults, validation, forwarding, and errors; exit-code meanings and mapping; supported platforms and platform-specific behavior; --help and --version behavior; and destructive-action safeguards such as dry-run, confirmation, and scope limits. Include applicable validation commands.

CLI README.md must add Commands and Exit codes, in that order, documenting installation, each user-facing command and important options, --help, --version, safe copyable examples, supported platform behavior, exit-code meanings, and destructive-action controls. Place these headings in the profile extension area defined by general.json and include them in the Table of Contents.
Every Discord application repository must extend the application AGENTS.md requirements with applicable Discord guidance.

After the seven general AGENTS.md headings, add a ## Discord section. Document Discord intents, commands, events, required permissions, runtime configuration, credential handling, lifecycle, and applicable validation commands.

Discord application README.md must add Commands, Events, Intents and permissions, and Operations, in that order, including safe startup/shutdown and deployment examples when supported. Operations merges with the application Operations heading required by application.json. Place these headings in the profile extension area defined by general.json and include them in the Table of Contents.
Every MCP server repository must extend the application AGENTS.md requirements with applicable MCP guidance.

After the seven general AGENTS.md headings, add a ## MCP server section. Document tools, resources, prompts, transport, authentication, schemas, protocol validation commands, and network/exposure boundaries.

MCP server README.md must add Tools, Resources, Prompts, Transport, Authentication, Schemas, and Operations, in that order, including Docker, Compose, or systemd examples when supported. Operations merges with the application Operations heading required by application.json. Place these headings in the profile extension area defined by general.json and include them in the Table of Contents.
The repository package version and the selected convention documents identify the convention baseline.
Crosslink relationship values must be dependsOn, consumedBy, relatedAuthority, implements, or supersedes.
Validation consumers must enforce the recorded eliware.exempt form: a concrete expiry date for temporary exemptions or expiry:null for permanent exemptions.
Validation consumers must validate exemption structure and rule applicability without re-reviewing, renewing, or second-guessing Eli's recorded exemption decision.
Every infrastructure repository must extend the general AGENTS.md requirements with applicable infrastructure guidance.
After the seven general AGENTS.md headings, add a ## Infrastructure section. Document managed targets, ownership boundaries, validation, change control, rollback, and secret handling.
AGENTS.md must distinguish committed desired state from operational procedures and live runtime evidence.
Keep committed desired state, declarative configuration, and deployment inputs in the infrastructure repository that owns them.
Keep operational procedures, rollout decisions, rollback records, and live runtime evidence in the applicable operations or owner workspace and link to them from the repository README.
Organize infrastructure content by managed target and environment where both dimensions exist.
Provide a deterministic validator for applicable syntax, schema, reference, render, and safety checks before promotion.
Keep repository-specific authority, directives, records, runbooks, and workflows in structured JSON when those records are required by the repository's authority boundary.
Use README.md and AGENTS.md as concise indexes and contributor instructions for those structured records.
Define subtype-specific requirements in the repository's own directive records when the repository manages Kubernetes, GitOps, VyOS, storage, or another specialized platform.

Infrastructure README.md must add Managed targets, Configuration, Desired state, Validation, and Change boundaries, in that order, documenting target/environment scope, runtime or deployment settings, committed desired state, deterministic checks, and change/rollback authority. Place these headings in the profile extension area defined by general.json and include them in the Table of Contents.
Infrastructure README.md must link operational procedures and live-state verification records without duplicating them.
Infrastructure repositories must declare required paths and files in their repository-specific directives or structured authority records.
Deterministic validation must verify each declared infrastructure path exists and validate its declared JSON, YAML, manifest, reference, or render schema.
Infrastructure validators must enforce repository structure, committed-input safety, and deterministic syntax or schema checks.
Keep platform-specific preflights, desired-state semantics, live-cluster behavior, and rollout or rollback execution in the owning repository or operations workspace.
These conventions apply to every @eliware/* repository.

Every maintained non-fork repository must contain a root AGENTS.md with the title # AGENTS.md followed by the exact general headings, in order: ## Project, ## Scope and boundaries, ## Layout, ## Development, ## Validation, ## Security, and ## Changes.

AGENTS.md must identify the repository and purpose, define scope and boundaries, explain the important layout, state development and validation expectations, define security rules, and state change/release authorization.
AGENTS.md must point contributors to applicable authority in eliware/docs, eliware/conventions, and eliware/operations without copying their detailed policy.

Keep the seven general AGENTS.md sections in the required order. Append applicable profile sections after ## Changes in this canonical order, omitting profiles that do not apply: application, cli, discord, mcp-server, web, library, infrastructure, workspace, documentation, npm-published, ghcr-published, private. The order of entries in package.json.eliware.apply determines applicability only and must not change document order. Append repository-specific authority, exception, subdirectory, or role sections after all profile sections only when their exact heading and purpose are explicitly declared in an authoritative repository-owned specification.
Every repository must contain a README.md file describing its purpose under Features and its intended use under Usage; a dedicated Purpose heading is not required.

Every maintained non-fork repository README must use this exact base order: Eliware logo header; package or project title with applicable npm, license, and CI badges; Table of Contents; Features; Requirements; Setup; Usage; Development; Testing; Troubleshooting; Security; then any sections added by applicable profiles; then Support; License; and Links. Support, License, and Links are always the final three top-level sections, in that order.
The README must use the standard Eliware logo and Discord-branded support block and link the repository LICENSE from License.

Build the README section list from the general baseline and every profile explicitly listed in package.json.eliware.apply. Append profile-required sections after Security and before Support, using this canonical profile order regardless of package.json array order: application, cli, discord, mcp-server, web, library, infrastructure, workspace, documentation, npm-published, ghcr-published. Omit profiles that do not apply; within each applied profile, preserve the order stated by that profile. If multiple profiles require a section with the same exact heading, use one section at the position of its first occurrence and combine the applicable required content there. Do not merge sections with different headings merely because their topics overlap.

The badge-bearing package or project title is the README title: place it immediately after the Eliware logo header and do not treat it as a content section or include it in the Table of Contents. Only blank lines may occur between the logo header, title, and Table of Contents; no prose, links, badges, or other content may precede the Table of Contents. The README may use only the general and applicable profile level-two section headings, plus an additional repository-specific level-two section only when its exact heading and purpose are explicitly declared in an authoritative repository-owned specification. Put other repository-specific material under an applicable existing section; do not invent discretionary level-two sections. Lower-level headings may organize material beneath an allowed level-two section. The Table of Contents must link every level-two section after the title exactly once, in document order.

The README must identify the project truthfully, link applicable documentation/specifications/examples and RELEASE_NOTES.md when present, and document only profiles that apply. Do not add prose saying unrelated profiles do not apply.
When package.json declares description, author, and license values, include each exact value verbatim in README.md. When package.json declares a repository URL, link that exact URL from Links.

Configuration content must distinguish runtime configuration (supported settings, environment variables, config files, and defaults) from repository/package metadata, CLI arguments, and deployment configuration. State explicitly when a category has no runtime settings; do not describe package.json.eliware.apply as runtime configuration.

When documenting validation or release state, distinguish checks and contracts present in the current repository from versions already published or released. Do not imply an unpublished version is available to users.
The npm badge and npm package link are required only for public npm packages; private and non-published repositories must not present npm publication identity.
Every repository must contain a Knit configuration and validation script.
Each repository's Knit configuration defines its own synchronization and validation commands.
Knit is secondary Linux validation and synchronization, not package or image publication, release execution, or production deployment.
Every applicable Knit validation script must begin its commands in this exact order: git pull --ff-only origin main, then npm ci, then npm test.
These Knit commands are limited to repository synchronization and validation; they must not add package or image publication, release, deployment, or destructive operations.
These conventions apply to documentation-only repositories.
Documentation-only repositories must provide the required documentation indexes and link each documented surface from the applicable root index.
Request application-specific web-service ports from the external Eliware port registry.
These conventions apply to workspace repositories.
Keep conventions focused on repository structure, files, contents, and deterministic repository validation.
External forks follow the upstream repository's own instructions, contribution rules, coding standards, and validation.
Use forks for upstream contributions.
Preserve the upstream remote, fork provenance, and contribution context.
Follow the fork's existing AGENTS.md, contribution guidelines, coding standards, validation, and submission process.
Verify upstream contribution status and review requirements before proposing work.
Obtain Eli's specific authorization before creating a pull request.
Do not retain compatibility layers, legacy behavior, deprecated aliases, or fallback implementations.
These conventions apply to repositories containing application or service code.
Every application repository must contain docs/README.md for end-user documentation.
For repositories with npm dependencies, npm outdated must return no outdated direct dependencies before release consideration.
Repositories that publish a public npm package must apply npm-published.json.
Public npm packages must set private to false.

After the seven general AGENTS.md headings, add a ## npm publication section. Document package identity and version source, exact files allowlist, pack validation command and required result, provenance mechanism, exact-version registry verification, and the release authorization/handoff boundary. Document release gates and who is authorized to approve or execute them, but do not treat this documentation or the profile as permission for an agent to publish. Publication still requires explicit authorization through the applicable Operations release handoff.

Public npm packages must declare engines.node compatible with Node.js 26, publishConfig.provenance true, and a non-empty files allowlist containing README.md, LICENSE, RELEASE_NOTES.md, docs/, and specs/.

Public npm package README.md must include the npm badge, npm package link, installation guidance, package entrypoints, and release/version guidance. When npm-published is applied without a library profile, include this material in Usage or an applicable profile section rather than inventing a library API section.

Public npm packages must define exactly `pack=eliware-test --pack` and must pass the harness pack stage during aggregate validation and before publication; their shared audit script is defined by general.json.
Use the latest stable published version of every direct dependency unless Eli approves a specific pin for that repository.
Private repositories must apply private.json and set package.json private to true.
Private repositories may publish authorized GHCR images without becoming npm packages.
After the seven general AGENTS.md headings, add a ## Private distribution section. Document private distribution restrictions, access boundaries, and non-public publication rules.
Align repository release versions with the convention baseline they implement.
Every repository that publishes an image to GHCR must apply ghcr-published.json in addition to general.json and its applicable public or private distribution profile.
GHCR publication is separate from general validation, npm publication, and deployment execution.

After the seven general AGENTS.md headings, add a ## GHCR publication section. Document image identity, visibility, publication workflow and required validation, provenance/signing mechanism, registry credential boundary, exact digest verification, and deployment-consumer boundary. Document release gates and the Operations handoff; do not treat this profile or its documentation as permission to publish.
A single-image repository must publish ghcr.io/eliware/<repository-name>.
A repository publishing multiple images must publish ghcr.io/eliware/<repository-name>-<image-name> for each image.
The project owner must propose the image mapping and Eli is the final approver with authority to override it.

GHCR repositories must contain exactly one publication workflow at .github/workflows/publish.yml in addition to .github/workflows/ci.yml; no other GitHub Actions workflow files are allowed. If npm publication is also applied, both publication profiles use this single publish.yml file.

GHCR publication workflows must use the GitHub Actions tag filter `v[0-9]+.[0-9]+.[0-9]+` so only three-component numeric version-shaped tags start the workflow; verify the tag and approved release version before pushing, and require Eli's explicit authorization routed through the Operations release handoff. The README must document the image name, pull command, supported tags, and deployment boundary; an approved GHCR badge may be added when a standard badge URL exists.

The GHCR publication workflow must be separate from the general validation workflow and must require successful Ubuntu validation using the inherited npm ci followed by npm test flow before publication.
A repository that also publishes npm must keep npm publication separate while reusing the inherited validation result and exact release identity.
The default GHCR authentication method must be the repository-scoped GITHUB_TOKEN with only contents: read and packages: write permissions for the publication job.

Every GHCR publication must generate a signed GitHub artifact attestation using actions/attest@v4 after the image push, with id-token: write, attestations: write, artifact-metadata: write, contents: read, and packages: write permissions as required by the attestation workflow.

The attestation must use the fully qualified image name without a tag and the pushed image digest as subject-digest, set push-to-registry: true, and record the attestation result with the release handoff.
The project owner must own the Dockerfile or equivalent build definition, build context, and supported-architecture declaration; DevOps executes the approved build and publication.
Single-architecture builds are the baseline; multi-architecture publication requires project-specific declaration and approval before implementation.
The exact version tag and recorded sha256 digest together identify the published image for release and deployment.
latest may be published only as a documented mutable convenience alias and must never be the release or deployment identity.

The publication workflow must expose the pushed image digest, verify that the exact version tag resolves to that digest, and verify that the image and signed attestation are readable according to the repository visibility before reporting publication success.
Every @eliware/* repository must keep source under src/ and mirror that structure under tests/ with exactly one corresponding .test.mjs file for every .mjs source file.
Place fixtures, snapshots, generators, and shared test support under artifacts/ when they have no source counterpart.
Place unit tests at the lowest module level that directly proves the behavior; keep only cross-cutting and integration tests in higher-level orchestrator test directories.
Classify production modules by responsibility and fully decompose broad orchestrators into focused modules without moving business logic into coordination code.
Every repository must contain package.json with a scoped @eliware/* name, version, description, keywords, author, repository, license: "MIT", and the repository's Jest configuration.
Every repository package.json must declare an engines.node requirement compatible with Node.js 26.
Package metadata must identify publication and file contents explicitly when the repository publishes a package.
Every repository must contain README.md at its root.
Every repository must contain specs/README.md as the index for its directive, authority, and repository-specific specification records.
Every @eliware/* repository must use Node.js package tooling and eliware-test for deterministic repository validation.
Maintained Node.js projects must use Node.js 26.
Jest coverage for every repository must report 100% statements, branches, functions, and lines with zero uncovered lines for in-scope production code.
In-scope code includes source implementation files; generated, bundled, compiled, dependency, coverage, build, declaration, fixture, and snapshot files are excluded.
The only source exclusion is a pure export barrel that is the primary public entrypoint of a library.
Before release consideration, repositories with npm dependencies must run npm outdated and have no outdated direct dependencies.
Use the latest stable published version of every direct dependency unless Eli approves a specific pin for that repository.
Repositories must remove dependencies that are not used by their source, tests, tooling, or required runtime.
Allow pure export barrels only when they are the primary public entrypoint or index of a library.
Keep each non-generated, non-dependency Node.js production source file at 100 lines or fewer and each non-generated, non-dependency test file at 200 lines or fewer.
Fully decompose files that exceed a threshold into focused modules and mirrored tests.

An Eli-approved emergency exemption must be recorded in package.json.eliware.exempt with this rule ID, reason, approver, approval timestamp, and either a concrete expiry date for a temporary exemption or expiry:null for a permanent exemption.

Every repository must define exactly these shared validation scripts: test=eliware-test, lint=eliware-test --lint, audit=eliware-test --audit, format=eliware-test --format, and format:check=eliware-test --format-check.
Every repository's aggregate test validation must execute its audit stage through the shared audit script.
Node.js projects must use native ESM exclusively.
Test execution must keep stdout and stderr quiet unless output is the subject of the test or is an intentional failure diagnostic.
Tests that exercise logging must inject a logger mock, capture the logger, or redirect stdout and stderr through the test boundary.
Node.js projects must keep entrypoints thin.
Each Node.js module must have one primary responsibility.
Use dependency injection to keep Node.js modules easily testable.
Use npm to regenerate package-lock.json whenever it is stale.
Repositories using Jest must keep Jest configuration in package.json.
Node.js repositories must include .env.example when they support environment configuration, documenting every supported variable, default, allowed value, and allowed range.
Projects and libraries must use the Eliware common stack modules for redaction, logging, paths, errors, and signals.
Use only E-rules at the top level of directive documents.
Nest every A-rule under an E- or A-rule with an E ancestor.
Nest E-rules only under E-rules.
Every @eliware/* repository must contain a LICENSE file using the MIT license with the attribution Copyright (c) 2026 Eliware.
Every @eliware/* repository must contain a GitHub Actions workflow that runs the repository's validation script on pull requests and pushes to main.

Every repository must contain exactly one workflow file at .github/workflows/ci.yml. Repositories must not contain any other GitHub Actions workflow files unless an applied publication profile explicitly requires .github/workflows/publish.yml.
Ubuntu CI is always required.
Windows CI is optional; when included, every Windows validation job must pass before publication.
The GitHub validation workflow may run the same validation command as .knit/validate.mjs.
Every GitHub Actions CI workflow must use the approved v6 major version for each required action, including actions/checkout and actions/setup-node when those actions are used.

An explicitly authorized future exception must be recorded in package.json.eliware.exempt with this rule ID, the exact action and version, reason, approver, and approvalTimestamp, and must be either temporary with a concrete expiry date or permanent with expiry:null.

Every active GitHub Actions CI validation workflow must declare top-level concurrency with a group key that includes github.repository and github.ref, or an equivalent key that uniquely identifies the repository and ref, and must set cancel-in-progress: true.
The concurrency control must cancel obsolete duplicate runs for the same repository and ref when a newer run supersedes them.

Every active GitHub Actions validation workflow must contain only repository validation steps plus required setup and non-publishing reporting steps; its validation flow is npm ci followed by npm test.
Publication workflows must be separate from the general validation workflow and governed by the applicable publication profile and Operations release policy.
Every repository must use specs/ as the discoverable home for its directive, authority, and repository-specific specification records.
Every application and library repository must maintain a root RELEASE_NOTES.md; other repository types must maintain one when they publish versioned user-visible changes.

RELEASE_NOTES.md must use the exact structure # Release Notes, ## Unreleased when pending work exists, and version headings in the form ## x.y.z — YYYY-MM-DD, with applicable Added, Changed, Fixed, Breaking changes, Migration, and Security subsections.
Repositories must use eliware-test for the shared Jest, Oxlint, and Prettier validation stack.
ESM test files may import the Jest APIs from @jest/globals; eliware-test supplies this API transitively, so the import does not replace the shared runner or authorize a direct Jest tool dependency.
Repositories must pass lint with zero errors and zero warnings.
These conventions apply to repositories containing library code.
Published libraries must validate the package contents and allowlist before publication.
Published libraries must run package dry-run validation and verify the resulting file allowlist before publication.
Libraries must define a non-empty typecheck script using the repository's direct typechecker and must pass `npm run typecheck` during aggregate validation and before release consideration.
Repositories must test all applicable code without Istanbul coverage-ignore directives.
These conventions apply to repositories containing web application code.
Web application repositories must also apply application.json.
Web applications must use public/ as the default public asset root and exclude dist/, build/, coverage/, node_modules/, and .git/ from public assets.
A web application may override the root only with eliware.webRoot as a non-empty package.json string and may declare exclusions only with eliware.webAssetExcludes as a string array.
Web projects that own browser, Lighthouse, smoke, live-system, or end-to-end acceptance checks must explicitly document the required checks and expected results for owner and QA review.
Web applications must define a non-empty build script using the repository's direct build tool and must pass `npm run build` during aggregate validation and before release consideration.
Web applications must declare Lighthouse and Puppeteer as direct dependencies and define `lighthouse` and `puppeteer` scripts that invoke those web-app-owned tools.

Web-specific Lighthouse and Puppeteer scripts are additional application checks; validation must verify their dependencies and script definitions but must not run them automatically because they require a live server.
Repositories must keep secrets, credentials, keys, tokens, .env files, generated sessions, and machine state out of version control.
Repositories must also exclude decrypted data, private conversations, operational database backups, production dumps, database state, restore archives, and runtime state.
Bootstrap schemas and minimal non-sensitive seed records are allowed when required for a fresh install; platform DBA and Storage owners retain backup, restore, retention, and recovery ownership.
These conventions apply to repositories containing CLI application code.
CLI application repositories must also apply application.json.

CLI applications must contain bin/ with the executable entrypoint, implement and document --help and --version, document exit codes and redacted output, and provide dry-run or confirmation controls for destructive actions.
Public repositories must keep Eliware infrastructure internals private.
These conventions apply to repositories containing Discord application code.
Discord application repositories must also apply application.json.
Every repository must define MAIL_OWNER_ADDRESS in its local untracked .env file as <repository-name>@eliware.org.
These conventions apply to repositories containing MCP server application code.
MCP server application repositories must also apply application.json.
Every Eliware repository package.json must contain an eliware object describing convention applicability, authority, and repository relationships.
package.json.eliware.apply must explicitly list applicable convention documents.
package.json.eliware.exempt may contain only Eli-approved emergency exemptions for explicitly exemptible rule IDs.
package.json.eliware.apply must explicitly list applicable convention documents.

Each eliware.exempt entry must reference a specific rule ID, contain a reason, Eli approver, approval timestamp, and declare either a concrete expiry date for a temporary exemption or expiry:null for a permanent exemption.
eliware.authority must contain non-empty authoritativeFor and notAuthoritativeFor arrays.
eliware.crosslinks must contain related repository paths, relationship types, and the authority represented by each link.
Forked upstream repositories may omit the Eliware metadata contract unless Eli explicitly authorizes Eliware convention adoption.
These conventions apply to repositories containing infrastructure code.
Keep infrastructure desired state, configuration layout, and committed deployment inputs in the owning infrastructure repository.
